fields.title: Bigger Server vs More Servers
fields.keyTakeaway: What does not store state scales horizontally, and the product growth ceiling is usually determined by the write database or someone else's limit.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Load doubled. Why in one case is the solution an hour of work, and in another — a quarter?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Products run into scaling ceilings suddenly: up to a certain point, growth was handled by buying a larger server, and it went unnoticed. A PM who knows where the ceiling is puts the work into the plan in advance; one who does not learns about it at the moment when growth has already happened.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: **[[scaling-up|Vertical scaling]]** — the same component on a more powerful machine. Requires no code changes, done in hours. Limited by a physical ceiling: the largest machine is finite, and the price grows non-linearly — twice as powerful costs four times as much.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **[[scaling-out|Horizontal scaling]]** — more machines. Virtually no ceiling, cost is linear. Requires the component to allow it.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: The condition for horizontal scaling is **[[stateless|statelessness]]**: the service remembers nothing between requests, any request can be handled by any instance. Then adding a machine is trivial.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: [[stateful|Stateful services]] scale poorly because state must be split or synchronized. The main one is the database, and that is precisely why it usually turns out to be the [[bottleneck|bottleneck]].
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: Hence the practical picture of most products:
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/3/1: Vertically to the ceiling, then sharding
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/4/1: Does not scale at all, limited by their limits
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: The last row is often missed: our ceiling can be determined by someone else's limit, and no amount of our hardware will change that.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Application services — horizontally, autoscaling by load. Growth here is not a problem.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: Database writes — vertically. Current server is loaded at 40% at peak, the next level provides about double the headroom, beyond that is user-key sharding, analyzed in `DS2-N5`.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: The real ceiling was not ours: the payment provider supports 200 transactions per second by contract. At a peak of 370 requests per second and a checkout share of about 4% — that is 15 transactions, plenty of headroom. But with a campaign doubling the peak and doubling conversion, the figure approaches 60, and during a sale it might hit the limit.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: Conclusion for planning: before major campaigns, not only our capacities are checked, but also provider limits. This is a separate checklist item.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Horizontal scaling is not free: more machines mean more network calls, more complex operations, more expensive debugging. As long as vertical scaling works, it is simpler.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: What does not store state scales horizontally, and the product growth ceiling is usually determined by the write database or someone else's limit.
